title: Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic in October 2026
excerpt: METR's high-access assessment of the degree to which AI is accelerating AI research and development at Anthropic.
content_html:
Redaction summary: As part of this assessment, Anthropic had rights to redact any non-public information in this post. Per our approach to transparency, we had the right to disclose if Anthropic exercised redaction rights, and whether or not any of our findings depended significantly on redacted information. While we were able to freely share our highest-level conclusions about risk, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative for these conclusions. Anthropic described the redactions as “aimed at removing confidential information that could accelerate other AI developers.”1 Some of these redactions are themselves challenging to describe clearly without revealing sensitive information we have been asked to redact. We share a table of important evidence we were and were not able to discuss given the redactions in our process section below. All redactions that were important for our conclusions are covered by our descriptions in that table or other in-line descriptions in the report below.

Much of the redacted evidence we viewed had multiple plausible interpretations, and both METR and Anthropic researchers have significant uncertainty about how to synthesize the evidence into a holistic picture. This makes it hard for the public to judge this evidence themselves, reconcile it with evidence from other sources, and come to their own conclusions (i.e. this report does not achieve ‘transparency about evidence’). As a consequence, the public has to rely on METR’s judgment much more than would be ideal, given the weight of the questions answered here.

Executive summary

From August 12 to October 29, 2026, METR staff performed a high-access evaluation at Anthropic to assess the degree to which AI is accelerating AI R&D.2 If AI systems started to significantly accelerate further AI development, this could lead to a sudden emergence of extreme and risky capabilities.

Anthropic offered unprecedented access to internal data on their AI R&D process, including a variety of metrics on pretraining, reinforcement learning (RL), training compute in each domain, benchmark scores for internal models, AI speedup analyses, forecasts of a future model’s metrics, and interviews with relevant staff.

In our first section, we share our subjective conclusions about risk. We now believe that:

  • As of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025. This estimate is given with high uncertainty; we would not be surprised if the true acceleration was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate.
  • A majority of this acceleration today is likely attributable to Anthropic’s extensive use of AI to do R&D, though there is significant uncertainty and other causes likely played a large role in acceleration in late 2025.
  • The lack of observed bottlenecks or strong diminishing returns means there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration, though, as we say below, we may be missing important bottlenecks.

In our second section we share some of the key empirical findings from our Full Report:

  • Since October 2025, benchmark scores (measured via AECI, Anthropic’s version of the Epoch Capabilities Index) for Anthropic’s models have been growing at an estimated 1.9x the pre-October 2025 rate [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x], implying that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year.
  • We are confident that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scaling of training compute.
  • Interviews and surveys are consistent with AI usage causing a doubling in the pace of capabilities progress. Anthropic staff self-report dramatic uplift from use of AI systems in interviews and surveys, although these are challenging to interpret. We were told that R&D is accelerated primarily via AI assistance rather than fully autonomous contributions, but there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.
  • We did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks which would prevent further capabilities progress due to limits on algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data in the next 12 months. However, our understanding of the status of different bottlenecks changed several times as we received more detailed information, so we are not confident in our current assessment.

Some of the key findings that most informed our conclusions about risk were redacted by Anthropic.

In our third section, we describe the assessment process:

  • The scope, setup, and timeline of this assessment.
  • Details of the information shared with METR.
  • Details of what information and evidence we were not able to share given Anthropic’s redactions.

Finally, we describe the biggest limitations of our analysis:

  • We could be underestimating capability acceleration if we did not assign enough importance to (1) evidence that some growth rates have further increased recently; (2) further automation of AI R&D tasks leading to a further acceleration in progress; (3) evidence that AECI growth has sometimes understated growth in real-world impact.
  • We could be overestimating capability acceleration if we did not assign enough importance to (1) non-AI factors in Anthropic’s research progress; (2) AECI’s focus on verifiable tasks; (3) reasons why Anthropic’s early growth rate (2023–2025) was unusually low.

The remainder of the report goes into detailed discussion of each of the key components. We include appendices with supplemental material.

Our subjective conclusions on risk

Our conclusions on risk.

Independently of this assessment, METR published an October 2026 article proposing a set of high-level questions about AI R&D acceleration we believe the public needs to understand to be able to judge loss-of-control risks from frontier AI development. In this section, we describe how the evidence we reviewed in this assessment changed our subjective conclusions on these high-level questions.

Pace of capabilities progress.

A significant acceleration of Anthropic’s overall rate of progress would be surprising, since diminishing returns and dependence on compute scaling mean this would likely require remarkable scaling in other inputs.3 After reviewing the internal evidence, we still have significant uncertainty and internal disagreements on the team, but most METR staff who worked on this project now believe that, as of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025. We would not be surprised if the current rate of growth was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate. We have additional uncertainty in how this acceleration translates to broader and less well-specified tasks.

The 1.9x acceleration [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x] in the AECI trend since October 2025 described below significantly informed this view, but could be explained by overfitting to the benchmark distribution or otherwise be an artifact of the AECI methodology. On the other hand, we are not confident that AECI would reliably let us estimate recent R&D acceleration, since the data points are lagging acceleration in research and are somewhat sparse.

Beyond the AECI evidence, we also saw redacted evidence that significantly informed our view on this question, and made us take this apparent ≈2x acceleration more seriously. It also gave us some indication that acceleration could be above 2x and increasing over time, though we would be surprised if it was significantly higher.

Attribution to AI.

We looked at a variety of factors that could explain the acceleration we observed, including compute scaling, hiring, data improvements, algorithmic discoveries, and resolving other bottlenecks.

As we describe below, we were able to confidently determine that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the rate of growth of training compute. Beyond that, there was not a consensus among Anthropic’s own staff and we did not find decisive evidence. Our overall subjective estimate is that:

  1. The acceleration in late 2025 was likely influenced by non-AI factors. We investigated a variety of factors which could have contributed to the observed acceleration in late 2025, but details of many of these factors have been redacted.
  2. We guess that a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current (October 2026) acceleration is due to AI. This judgment is given with substantial uncertainty, but is based on a variety of lines of evidence on contributions from AI and other causes. We believe AI’s contribution has grown relatively more important over time, and do not think the other factors we investigated would explain the sustained acceleration. The evidence of speedup from the usage of AI we describe below also seems compatible with a large contribution.

We illustrate these points below:

Our more detailed estimates for the cumulative and instantaneous effects of AI on Anthropic’s rate of progress in AECI, and at various stages of the model training pipeline, were redacted.

Bottlenecks to further acceleration.

A key concern is that acceleration from the use of AI could start to compound, as the development of more capable models leads to further acceleration. As we describe below, we did not identify any clear bottlenecks (limited inputs that would prevent further growth) or steep diminishing returns to further scaling that would get in the way of such compounding acceleration, though our understanding evolved several times over the course of this assessment, and we have significant uncertainty. Because of this, we believe there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration over the coming year.

Key findings

In this section, we summarize the key empirical findings from our Full Report that we can describe without revealing redacted information (see the process section for more details on what was redacted).

Terminology: We describe growth as annual multiples and acceleration as a ratio of growth rates.

We use “acceleration” to refer to an increase in the rate of growth, such that a 2x acceleration means that 2 years of historical progress is made in 1 year.

If AECI’s historical trend was 15 points/year, then increasing to 30 points/year implies an acceleration rate of 2 (it takes 1 year to achieve 2 years’ progress at the old rate). For an exponentially growing variable, the acceleration rate is the ratio of growth rates. If a variable is growing 3x/year, then to make 2 years of progress in 1 year the growth rate must be (32)x/yr = 9x/yr (and acceleration can be written as ln(9)/ln(3) = 2).

Since October 2025, benchmark scores for internal models have been growing at around twice their historical rate.

Benchmark scores of Anthropic’s models, as measured by AECI (Anthropic’s version of the Epoch Capabilities Index), have accelerated 1.9x [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x] since October 2025. Put another way, Anthropic appears to have made as much progress on benchmarks in the past year as they did between October 2023 and October 2025 (roughly, Claude 2.1 to Sonnet 4.5):

Our estimated acceleration is greater than that reported in the Haiku 5.5 system card (1.7x) primarily because of the inclusion of data on newer unreleased models, explained further below.

We investigated the robustness of these results to different choices of benchmark inclusion, model dating, model inclusion, and benchmark saturation. Robustness analyses find acceleration rates between 1.1x and 2.9x. We would be surprised if the true evolution of benchmark scores (e.g. as measured by an improved version of AECI) showed no acceleration or acceleration above 3x. See our appendix section for details.

The acceleration is not driven by an acceleration in the scale of training compute.

We received convincing evidence that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scale of training compute. Further details on this evidence were redacted.

Interviews and surveys are consistent with AI usage driving this doubling in the pace of capabilities progress.

We have many lines of evidence relevant to AI’s contribution to progress in different parts of the model training pipeline, including interviews, self-reported uplift, headcount, lines of code, experiment usage, and qualitative reflections from leadership. We highlight three important unredacted sources.

First, both METR and Anthropic interviewed many researchers in detail about the degree of overall acceleration in their area of work attributable to AI use (see details in the appendix below). Our overall impression was a quite wide range of estimates, but centered around a 2x acceleration. Some quotes, with sensitive details redacted, are in the appendix.

Second, Anthropic also shared data on self-reported uplift due to AI from a variety of sources. The most recent data is from a series of Slack polls, where staff use reactions to vote on their estimated speedup from the most recent model at the time. We consider this to be only very loose evidence, as the responses reflect low-effort consideration. Nevertheless, we observe consistent growth in these self-reports, and very high levels (reaching 12x in October 2026), as shown in the chart below.

Note that individual uplift/speedup estimates do not correspond to acceleration rates. Sustaining a particular growth rate in outputs like model capabilities generally requires a similarly sustained growth in inputs like labor and/or labor productivity to overcome diminishing returns. Achieving a significant acceleration in the overall rate of progress generally requires a significant acceleration of these inputs. We thus care most about whether we see a large change in the growth rate of individual uplift, not the absolute level. Our more detailed analysis of what rate of growth in individual uplift might be needed to explain our estimated acceleration rates in key areas was redacted.

Third, we understand that AI is not yet able to make highly significant and fully autonomous contributions to the most important parts of the model training process. However, researchers described significant “signs of life” implying such contributions could occur soon, although with substantial variation in maturity depending on the area.

We did not identify any convincing bottlenecks to continued rapid progress.

We did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks in algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data that will take effect in the next 12 months. However, our understanding of the status of different bottlenecks changed several times as we got more detailed information, so we are not confident in our current assessment. Anthropic redacted our analysis of a number of specific bottlenecks.

Additional redacted evidence was sometimes hard to interpret, but supports sustained and potentially increasing acceleration.

We investigated a number of internal metrics and methodologies for measuring acceleration in key areas of the model training pipeline. This included evidence of progress on benchmarks and metrics of algorithmic efficiency and overall model strength in pretraining and RL, as well as improvements to compute utilization, inference efficiency and data efficiency. These investigations included attempts to understand:

  1. Different methodological variants of internal metrics. We spent multiple weeks on these investigations, and this is our greatest source of uncertainty.
  2. The beliefs of staff on the relevant teams about key internal evidence and estimates of acceleration.
  3. Whether other parts of the model training pipeline could be biasing our estimates of acceleration, and where adjustments could be applied.
  4. Whether Anthropic could be overfitting to internal metrics.

This internal evidence provided support for there being significant acceleration in Anthropic’s model training pipeline. Some of this evidence indicated that acceleration could be above 2x and increasing over time, but there are significant uncertainties about how to interpret it.

Process details

METR staff assessed how much AI is speeding up AI R&D at Anthropic.

METR staff4 (2.5 full-time equivalents) piloted a high-access evaluation at Anthropic to assess the degree to which AI is accelerating AI R&D, and how quickly extreme and risky capabilities may emerge in the near future.

Anthropic lists AI R&D acceleration as a key risk indicator in its Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP). In this assessment, we do not pay special attention to the thresholds set in the RSP. Instead, we try to develop a holistic picture of AI-driven acceleration of AI R&D.

This engagement started in mid-August, and is distinct from the assessment announced on October 15 by Anthropic.

Details of the engagement.

The METR staff worked over eleven weeks to independently assess how much AI is accelerating AI R&D at Anthropic. Our assessment focused on three broad questions:

  1. Has the growth rate of Anthropic’s internal capabilities accelerated?
  2. What share of any acceleration is attributable to AI?
  3. Are there important bottlenecks that could slow growth or limit acceleration in the near term?

We were additionally scoped to review the AI R&D section of Anthropic’s August 2026 Risk Report, which we are publishing separately. As we describe below, the initial contracted assessment was scoped to include a verification of what percent of compute was allocated to capabilities vs. safety.

METR had the ability to request access to any information we believed relevant to understanding AI R&D acceleration, and Anthropic could unilaterally approve or reject our requests. In practice, we often negotiated with Anthropic staff and compromised towards data that was informative, not extremely sensitive, and easy to share. We give more details on what Anthropic shared as well as what it declined to share below, noting that broadly the access provided surpassed our expectations. For this engagement, we did not request or receive access to sample from non-public models.

Note that neither METR nor Anthropic intended for this project to involve full “employee-like” access, meaning unmediated access to data, documents, or models. In particular, this project is not the one described in Anthropic’s October 15 update on independent evaluators.

Anthropic had unilateral redaction rights over all non-public information in this report. We had a unilateral right to disclose:

  • the existence and general terms of the review and redaction process,
  • whether Anthropic exercised redaction rights,
  • whether or not any findings depended significantly on redacted information,
  • the level of access provided.

For security reasons, we worked on Anthropic devices for the duration of this assessment. Anthropic provided free tokens for this assessment, which we primarily used for AI-assisted data analysis and visualization. Per our standard approach, we did not take payment from Anthropic.

This exercise followed METR’s policies for engaging with AI companies. We provide a conflict of interest (COI) disclosure and excerpted contract language in the process transparency disclosures appendix plus the AEF-1 checklist.

Details of Anthropic’s redactions.

Our ~100-page Full Report attempts to answer the key questions we recently described as crucial to answer in future AI R&D assessments in detail. We summarize the evidence sources we were given, and which we were able to include in this public report, in the table below.

Anthropic’s redactions also meant that we could not communicate:

  1. Our more detailed estimates of acceleration and attribution to AI usage for key areas of the model training pipeline.
  2. Our more detailed breakdown of progress attributable to compute, data and algorithmic progress, other than the key takeaway that “We are confident that the acceleration was not due to acceleration in training compute.”
  3. More detailed answers to the limitations questions in our proposal, which would require more discussion of methodological details.
  4. Forecasts of metrics for future models.

They also made some other more minor redactions throughout, which we attempt to describe in each section of this report.

Anthropic described the redactions as “aimed at removing confidential information that could accelerate other AI developers.”

  2. August 14: Anthropic shares the unredacted version of its August AI R&D Risk Report with METR.
  3. September 12: METR delivers a first draft of its Full Report to Anthropic for feedback.

METR received a significant amount of private data from Anthropic.

METR made extensive requests for information on every part of the AI R&D pipeline, and Anthropic shared more information than was initially scoped for this project, surpassing our expectations. Information was typically shared within a few days of requesting it.

A detailed description of the data we had access to was redacted. A summarized version is as follows:

  1. Internal benchmark scores and AECI for internal models, plus sample tasks, rubric answers and agent expenditure on those tasks.
  2. Historical data on algorithmic efficiency and overall model strength in pretraining and RL, as well as improvements to compute utilization, inference efficiency and data efficiency.
  3. Headcount and attribution of progress to specific staff.
  4. Training compute metrics in many relevant domains.
  5. Internal analysis on relevant open questions.
  6. Internal surveys of self-reported AI uplift by team.
  7. Lines of code and pull requests across the company and some research teams.
  8. AI agent inference spend over time.
  9. Internal documents on autonomous research contributions.
  10. ~15 interviews with key staff, covering a predefined but wide scope that excluded particularly sensitive topics.

In a small number of cases, Anthropic did not provide relevant information when they deemed it too sensitive.

Anthropic also offered extensive staff time and expertise to this project. We believe the two staff we worked most closely with are the two highest-context researchers on AI R&D acceleration measurement at Anthropic. Both of these staff met with us frequently for live discussion, and spent substantial time collecting data, doing analysis, and providing feedback.

Anthropic canceled a compute allocation component of this assessment.

The contracted scope of this project originally included a verification of Anthropic’s compute allocation, especially the allocation between capabilities and safety. However, Anthropic changed the scope of this project midway to exclude compute verification and instead just focus on AI R&D acceleration. This component was canceled before METR came to any substantive conclusions on compute usage at Anthropic. Anthropic stated this was due to wanting to keep the engagement focused on risk assessment for the time being, and that it would revisit compute allocation verification later on.

Limitations

We report our best guesses at ways in which we could be misinterpreting the evidence.

We discuss the main ways we could be making mistakes in our interpretation of the evidence. We highlight:

  1. Limitations that result from the structure of this assessment.
  2. Limitations that result from incorrect analysis.

Limited access may have led us to miss important context or data.

Despite the access provided to METR, it is clear that staff-level access would enable a significantly deeper assessment. Our pipeline of information was relatively narrow, and a small number of our requests for data were denied. Being able to read documents on demand, observe internal discussion and debate, and have frequent and diverse conversations would have allowed for a richer view. While we believe we had access to the bulk of relevant information, it is possible we missed important information because we did not know it existed or could not look for it ourselves.

Over the course of our exercise, we substantially changed our interpretation of key data as more context was shared with us, in some cases leading to multiple reversals on critical questions. We believe fuller access would have dramatically sped up that process of proper interpretation, and we think there likely remain points which we may have misinterpreted due to insufficient context.

Acceleration could be higher than this report estimates.

Our best guesses as to how we might be underestimating acceleration:

  1. We may have missed recent further acceleration. The rate of growth could be undergoing continuous acceleration, e.g. hyperbolic growth. While we do not see clear evidence of this in the AECI trends, there is other evidence that makes this seem more plausible which Anthropic redacted. If growth is hyperbolic, we are likely underestimating instantaneous acceleration and substantially understating acceleration in the near future. In addition, we observe model-level outcomes only after a model is trained, meaning we observe acceleration in effective R&D with a lag roughly equal to the model’s training time.
  2. Automation could be closer than we estimated. We understand that AI cannot yet fully automate substantial parts of Anthropic’s model training pipeline; however, there are “signs of life,” discussed below. It is possible that automation is close, and leads to very rapid acceleration once human bottlenecks are removed.
  3. AECI could understate real-world capability impact. We have sparse data on the relationship between benchmark scores and real-world impact. As one example, ECI scores on math have not accelerated substantially, but we are now seeing the resolution of Millennium Prize Problems that have evaded decades of human effort. Real-world impacts may be downstream of capability thresholds that models suddenly pass, leading to sudden impacts that are hard to predict.

Acceleration could be lower than this report estimates.

Our best guesses as to how we might be overestimating acceleration:

  1. Non-AI factors could explain most of the acceleration. It’s possible that the non-AI factors explain all or most of the recent acceleration. This implies we have less reason to expect high future growth or future accelerations.
  2. Acceleration might be limited to well-specified tasks. Much of the evidence we looked at measures performance on well-specified tasks that are easy to grade automatically or with a language model. If recent models have been growing more quickly on “clean” tasks than on “messy” tasks (relative to historical relative growth rates), then we may be overstating the acceleration in real-world impact. For instance, recent progress may be overfitting to the types of tasks which are included in AECI.
  3. Our acceleration numbers could be overstated if the historical rate of growth was unusually low. If progress historically was below its normal or natural rate due to temporary factors, this could lead us to overestimate the amount of acceleration. As we describe in an appendix, Anthropic models had a lower historical growth rate on AECI than the broader industry frontier before late 2025, which could explain some of the acceleration.

Appendices

Methodology

Redactions in this section.

None of this section was redacted, but note that some of the methodological discussion may only apply to the Full Report.

We include data from Anthropic internal-only models.

This includes the following models (these are the codenames shared with us; we understand they have different internal codenames):

  • Unreleased 2022, which finished training in 2022
  • Model 2, which finished training in July 2026
  • Model 3, which finished training in August–September 2026
  • Model 4, which finished training in September–October 2026

METR’s Full Report includes a forecast for a future model, but this was redacted.

We use piecewise linear fits to detect acceleration.

We typically estimate time trends by an ordinary least squares fit with a single estimated breakpoint; we then report acceleration as the ratio of the two estimated linear trends. We adopt the best-fitting breakpoint on standard AECI data as our default breakpoint on other graphs, to create a consistent breakpoint throughout this report. However, in some places we consider deviations from this, and test estimated acceleration as per the best fit on each graph.

We organize our analysis around 3 growth rates: the historical growth rate, the current growth rate and the counterfactual growth rate.

We want to assess the degree to which AI automation is speeding up AI progress. For any measure of progress (e.g. model capabilities as measured by AECI), we can estimate three numbers:

  1. Historical growth rate: the growth rate prior to a detected trend change.
  2. Current growth rate: the growth rate as of October 2026.
  3. Counterfactual growth rate: the growth rate as of October 2026, if Anthropic could not use AI.

The first two are observable quantities. The counterfactual growth rate we can only guess at. The following plot illustrates these measures on illustrative data:

It is important to distinguish between instantaneous acceleration due to AI, as we have defined it, and cumulative acceleration due to AI, i.e. what fraction of overall progress since some point in time (e.g. October 2025) can be attributed to AI. Some interviews and documents are implicitly or explicitly discussing cumulative acceleration, though we generally expect cumulative acceleration to be lower than instantaneous acceleration, due to non-AI acceleratory factors in 2025, and due to the growing influence of AI over time.

In the Full Report, we organize indirect evidence with a simple accounting framework.

We want to understand if there has been an acceleration in overall capabilities due to AI R&D. To reach our subjective conclusions, we organized our evidence using the following accounting framework, but all relevant usage of it was redacted.

Arrows into a box indicate that box is a function of the preceding boxes, so for example, pretraining strength is a function of algorithms, data quality, and training compute. We use the term RL to include all contributions not included in pretraining.

This framework lets us start at the right (capabilities) and determine whether there has been an acceleration. Then we can go back one level to see if there has been an acceleration in pretraining or RL, and then go back one further level to see what inputs are causing that acceleration. This allows us to get a deeper understanding of what is happening to the inputs.

In the Full Report, analyses were all documented in an accompanying notebook and dashboard.

For reproducibility we maintained a notebook and dashboard with all results in the Full Report. Where feasible we included references to the notebook or dashboard, and most charts had a “stamp” which identified their provenance.

Benchmark scores (AECI)

AECI appendix overview.

We expand on the main AECI analysis in a few ways.

  1. We explain the methodology behind our main estimation of a 1.9x acceleration in AECI.
  2. We show the degree of estimated acceleration varies based on reasonable alternative analysis choices:
    • Varying the link function: 1.1x–2.9x.
    • Varying the snapshots used: 1.9x–2.2x.
    • Varying the benchmarks used: 1.9x–2.2x.
    • Varying the regularizer used: 1.9x–2.1x.
  3. We explain why these results differ from AECI estimates in previous Anthropic system cards.
  4. We go into detail on potential problems with AECI such as:
    1. Anthropic’s internal benchmarks are increasingly saturated: Model 4 achieves greater than 50% on all the AECI benchmarks on which it was tested. However, measured acceleration appears reasonably robust to saturation concerns.
    2. Token spend may be too low to maximally elicit models.
    3. The logistic link function could be misspecified on a few benchmarks. However, on the whole we think it is a reasonable approximation.
    4. There are various reasons why an acceleration in benchmark scores could overstate or understate an acceleration in real-world impacts.

Redactions in this section.

This section was very minimally redacted by Anthropic. The only information redacted was:

  1. The names of specific benchmarks.
  2. One graph that shows AECI results for a subset of models chosen on the basis of information that is redacted.

Methodological details on AECI estimation.

We use Epoch’s public code to estimate AECI values for each model. We generate 95% confidence intervals via bootstrap by drawing benchmark scores with replacement, stratified by model.

Our underlying data includes the AECI scores of many snapshots per model. These snapshots differ in both dates and AECI scores.

For publicly released models, we include the snapshot that was publicly released and the date that snapshot was available for use by most Anthropic employees. For example, if a model has two snapshots: one available to Anthropic employees on November 10 and one available to Anthropic employees on November 20, and the second snapshot was released publicly on December 1, then our procedure would assign November 20 as the release date. We think there are many reasonable alternative dating procedures (e.g. at first snapshot release instead of last snapshot), which are shown below in one of the robustness exercises.

For models that are never released, we include snapshots that received substantial internal usage and the date most Anthropic employees could use them.

We use the date at which the model could be used by most Anthropic employees instead of public release dates; this allows us to make apples-to-apples comparisons with unreleased models. These in general show slightly higher degrees of acceleration as Anthropic is holding onto more recent models for slightly longer before their public release.

When we fit trends over time we use ordinary least squares with equal weight to each snapshot on the frontier. The confidence interval in the trend estimation only accounts for uncertainty in the AECI scores for each model, and does not include sampling uncertainty over which models are included in the fit.

We estimate a learned breakpoint in the trend, though we exogenously impose that there is 1 breakpoint. We estimate the breakpoint is October 7, 2025 in our main AECI specification. For our robustness checks, we maintain this October 7, 2025 breakpoint to ensure comparability.

Robustness: Estimates of AECI acceleration vary 1.1x–2.9x depending on the link function.

We show below that estimates of AECI acceleration are somewhat sensitive to assumptions about the distribution of task difficulty within each benchmark. In principle, we could discriminate between these assumptions based on the data, but in practice most functions fit the data about equally well. We acknowledge useful suggestions from Anthropic staff on analysis here.

AECI assumes that a model’s score on a benchmark is a function of the model’s latent strength, and specifically that the function is logistic (shown below in black). This can be interpreted as an assumption on the distribution of difficulty of tasks in a benchmark, including how many tasks are broken or what fraction can be guessed. The following figure illustrates a few different link functions. The logistic function assumes a symmetric distribution with exponentially declining tails. The log-log function assumes a long tail of hard tasks; the complementary log-log function assumes a long tail of easy tasks.

Model 4 achieves >50% on all of its benchmarks.

The plot below shows all benchmark scores for frontier models in the AECI, scaled on a log-odds scale, implying that they should evolve linearly with a model’s latent AECI score (if the logistic assumption holds). The highlighted lines represent the 15 benchmarks used for Model 4. Notably, Model 4 scores above 50% on all these benchmarks. We can see that the distribution of benchmark difficulty was very different just 9 months ago: Opus 4.6 had many benchmarks on which it scored below 50%. This lack of benchmarks which are difficult for Model 4 makes us somewhat nervous about our ability to measure AECI now and in the future.

Most of the benchmarks used for Model 4 appear reasonably linear in log-odds space.

A specific concern in measuring acceleration with AECI is benchmarks with many broken tasks, or benchmarks with a fat-tailed distribution of task difficulty. The logistic link function assumes exponential tails of task difficulty; if we instead had a fat-tailed distribution of task difficulty, this would mean that going from 98% to 99% requires more AECI points than going from 80% to 90% (the logistic assumes they are approximately equally difficult). A fat-tailed distribution of task difficulty could cause us to underestimate acceleration; as described above, using cauchit or log-log link functions (which model the last few tasks in a benchmark as particularly difficult) results in acceleration estimates of 2.8x and 2.9x, respectively.

We perform a simple diagnostic test for task difficulty. For each of the 15 benchmarks used for Model 4 in AECI, we compared a model’s estimated AECI against the model’s log-odds score on that benchmark. If the AECI assumptions are satisfied, meaning task difficulty is logistic in a model’s latent ability, then we would expect each plot to be linear. If there are many broken tasks or a fat-tailed distribution of difficulty, then we would expect these fits to be concave (we would expect a convex fit if there are disproportionately many easy tasks).

We noticed there are 3 of 15 benchmarks with notably flat or concave fits. When we re-estimate AECI for all models without those 3 suspicious benchmarks, Model 4’s score increases by 1 point, from 178.6 to 179.7. We thus think there is some weak evidence for fat tails causing understatement in acceleration, but the magnitude is not large.

Tokens per benchmark may be too low.

Using a low expenditure in benchmarking could bias estimates of capability growth downwards if later models show higher returns to expenditure (i.e. if early models plateau with expenditure, but later models show high returns).

Anthropic shared with us data on tokens used on benchmarks in the AECI. A typical task (one attempt) used about 2.5M input and 72k output tokens across internal benchmarks, and about 10M input and 94k output on agentic coding benchmarks. For a loose comparison, Epoch AI uses roughly 0.5M input and 10k output tokens on a typical task across a few public benchmarks (GPQA, AIME, SWE-bench), and 1M input and 8k output tokens on a specific agentic coding benchmark (SWE-bench). For another loose comparison, METR uses roughly 650k output tokens for its latest long-running software benchmarks, though it is possible the token accounting is not comparable.

Moreover, it would be informative to see returns-to-expenditure curves for each model, i.e. scores elicited at different levels of expenditure. Anthropic’s system cards do report expenditure curves for some benchmarks (e.g. Opus 5.5 system card). There is some recent evidence that it is possible to use very large amounts of inference compute to solve difficult problems (e.g. Navier–Stokes). Overall, our guess is that the AECI scores for each model could be increased by a handful of points if inference tokens were scaled further. Our rough guess is that this would have similar returns across models, so the degree of estimated acceleration would be the same, though this is not something we looked into deeply and it is possible that recent models have better token scaling properties.

An acceleration in benchmark scores may fail to track acceleration in real-world impact.

Ideally we want to know the real-world value, or potential impact, of each model, not its benchmark scores. If real-world impact is smoothly related to benchmark scores, then we should expect an acceleration in AECI to be associated with an equivalent acceleration in real-world effects.5

There are a number of reasons why acceleration in AECI may fail to track acceleration in the real-world impact of model capabilities:

  1. If real-world impact is a convex function of benchmark scores, e.g. if impact depends on crossing a capability threshold, then AECI would understate real-world acceleration. In some domains we have seen a steady increase in benchmark scores accompanied by sudden accelerations in real-world impacts, e.g. impacts on the rate of discoveries in cybersecurity or math (ref).
  2. If the benchmarks in AECI cover only a subset of capabilities, and the real-world impact has diminishing returns in those capabilities, then AECI could overstate real-world acceleration. For example, suppose AECI primarily measures a model’s ability to solve formal problems, but there are diminishing real-world returns in that ability; then we might observe an acceleration in AECI without an acceleration in real-world impact.

Overall, we are confident there has been at least a modest acceleration in the growth of benchmark scores. We believe there is significant risk that acceleration in AECI may not map cleanly to acceleration in real-world impact.

Adversarial robustness

We believe this exercise was reasonably adversarially robust.

As this is an independent assessment, it is important for us to do our due diligence and understand how hard it would have been for Anthropic to systematically mislead us, i.e., how likely it is that we could have been led to an incorrect conclusion intentionally.

Adversarial robustness weakness 1: We relied on data from a few Anthropic employees. Most of our data was received through two technical staff members; however, we interviewed around 15 other Anthropic employees on a range of topics. We did not notice any discrepancies between what our primary contacts said and what our interviewees said. Given that many of these Anthropic employees were chosen by us, not Anthropic, we think this would have been challenging to pull off if we were being given purposefully misleading information.

Adversarial robustness weakness 2: Most analysis relied on Claude. Claude was involved in many stages of this project, and so in principle could be distorting our perception of the data. We believe Claude was deeply involved in:

  • the majority of data collection and analysis that we received,
  • writing a significant share of the documents we received,
  • the majority of our own analysis.

We did not detect any significant discrepancies consistent with a systematic bias even when checking against human interviews. We suspect this is not a significant risk.

Overall, we think it is extremely unlikely Anthropic was actively trying to mislead us. However, we believe greater access would allow us to increase the degree of adversarial robustness.

content_text: Redaction summary: As part of this assessment, Anthropic had rights to redact any non-public information in this post. Per our approach to transparency, we had the right to disclose if Anthropic exercised redaction rights, and whether or not any of our findings depended significantly on redacted information. While we were able to freely share our highest-level conclusions about risk, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative for these conclusions. Anthropic described the redactions as “aimed at removing confidential information that could accelerate other AI developers.”1 Some of these redactions are themselves challenging to describe clearly without revealing sensitive information we have been asked to redact. We share a table of important evidence we were and were not able to discuss given the redactions in our process section below. All redactions that were important for our conclusions are covered by our descriptions in that table or other in-line descriptions in the report below. Much of the redacted evidence we viewed had multiple plausible interpretations, and both METR and Anthropic researchers have significant uncertainty about how to synthesize the evidence into a holistic picture. This makes it hard for the public to judge this evidence themselves, reconcile it with evidence from other sources, and come to their own conclusions (i.e. this report does not achieve ‘transparency about evidence’). As a consequence, the public has to rely on METR’s judgment much more than would be ideal, given the weight of the questions answered here. Executive summary From August 12 to October 29, 2026, METR staff performed a high-access evaluation at Anthropic to assess the degree to which AI is accelerating AI R&D.2 If AI systems started to significantly accelerate further AI development, this could lead to a sudden emergence of extreme and risky capabilities. Anthropic offered unprecedented access to internal data on their AI R&D process, including a variety of metrics on pretraining, reinforcement learning (RL), training compute in each domain, benchmark scores for internal models, AI speedup analyses, forecasts of a future model’s metrics, and interviews with relevant staff. In our first section, we share our subjective conclusions about risk. We now believe that: As of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025. This estimate is given with high uncertainty; we would not be surprised if the true acceleration was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate. A majority of this acceleration today is likely attributable to Anthropic’s extensive use of AI to do R&D, though there is significant uncertainty and other causes likely played a large role in acceleration in late 2025. The lack of observed bottlenecks or strong diminishing returns means there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration, though, as we say below, we may be missing important bottlenecks. In our second section we share some of the key empirical findings from our Full Report: Since October 2025, benchmark scores (measured via AECI, Anthropic’s version of the Epoch Capabilities Index) for Anthropic’s models have been growing at an estimated 1.9x the pre-October 2025 rate [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x], implying that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year. We are confident that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scaling of training compute. Interviews and surveys are consistent with AI usage causing a doubling in the pace of capabilities progress. Anthropic staff self-report dramatic uplift from use of AI systems in interviews and surveys, although these are challenging to interpret. We were told that R&D is accelerated primarily via AI assistance rather than fully autonomous contributions, but there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon. We did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks which would prevent further capabilities progress due to limits on algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data in the next 12 months. However, our understanding of the status of different bottlenecks changed several times as we received more detailed information, so we are not confident in our current assessment. Some of the key findings that most informed our conclusions about risk were redacted by Anthropic. In our third section, we describe the assessment process: The scope, setup, and timeline of this assessment. Details of the information shared with METR. Details of what information and evidence we were not able to share given Anthropic’s redactions. Finally, we describe the biggest limitations of our analysis: We could be underestimating capability acceleration if we did not assign enough importance to (1) evidence that some growth rates have further increased recently; (2) further automation of AI R&D tasks leading to a further acceleration in progress; (3) evidence that AECI growth has sometimes understated growth in real-world impact. We could be overestimating capability acceleration if we did not assign enough importance to (1) non-AI factors in Anthropic’s research progress; (2) AECI’s focus on verifiable tasks; (3) reasons why Anthropic’s early growth rate (2023–2025) was unusually low. The remainder of the report goes into detailed discussion of each of the key components. We include appendices with supplemental material. Our subjective conclusions on risk Our conclusions on risk. Independently of this assessment, METR published an October 2026 article proposing a set of high-level questions about AI R&D acceleration we believe the public needs to understand to be able to judge loss-of-control risks from frontier AI development. In this section, we describe how the evidence we reviewed in this assessment changed our subjective conclusions on these high-level questions. Pace of capabilities progress. A significant acceleration of Anthropic’s overall rate of progress would be surprising, since diminishing returns and dependence on compute scaling mean this would likely require remarkable scaling in other inputs.3 After reviewing the internal evidence, we still have significant uncertainty and internal disagreements on the team, but most METR staff who worked on this project now believe that, as of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025. We would not be surprised if the current rate of growth was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate. We have additional uncertainty in how this acceleration translates to broader and less well-specified tasks. The 1.9x acceleration [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x] in the AECI trend since October 2025 described below significantly informed this view, but could be explained by overfitting to the benchmark distribution or otherwise be an artifact of the AECI methodology. On the other hand, we are not confident that AECI would reliably let us estimate recent R&D acceleration, since the data points are lagging acceleration in research and are somewhat sparse. Beyond the AECI evidence, we also saw redacted evidence that significantly informed our view on this question, and made us take this apparent ≈2x acceleration more seriously. It also gave us some indication that acceleration could be above 2x and increasing over time, though we would be surprised if it was significantly higher. Attribution to AI. We looked at a variety of factors that could explain the acceleration we observed, including compute scaling, hiring, data improvements, algorithmic discoveries, and resolving other bottlenecks. As we describe below, we were able to confidently determine that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the rate of growth of training compute. Beyond that, there was not a consensus among Anthropic’s own staff and we did not find decisive evidence. Our overall subjective estimate is that: The acceleration in late 2025 was likely influenced by non-AI factors. We investigated a variety of factors which could have contributed to the observed acceleration in late 2025, but details of many of these factors have been redacted. We guess that a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current (October 2026) acceleration is due to AI. This judgment is given with substantial uncertainty, but is based on a variety of lines of evidence on contributions from AI and other causes. We believe AI’s contribution has grown relatively more important over time, and do not think the other factors we investigated would explain the sustained acceleration. The evidence of speedup from the usage of AI we describe below also seems compatible with a large contribution. We illustrate these points below: Our more detailed estimates for the cumulative and instantaneous effects of AI on Anthropic’s rate of progress in AECI, and at various stages of the model training pipeline, were redacted. Bottlenecks to further acceleration. A key concern is that acceleration from the use of AI could start to compound, as the development of more capable models leads to further acceleration. As we describe below, we did not identify any clear bottlenecks (limited inputs that would prevent further growth) or steep diminishing returns to further scaling that would get in the way of such compounding acceleration, though our understanding evolved several times over the course of this assessment, and we have significant uncertainty. Because of this, we believe there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration over the coming year. Key findings In this section, we summarize the key empirical findings from our Full Report that we can describe without revealing redacted information (see the process section for more details on what was redacted). Terminology: We describe growth as annual multiples and acceleration as a ratio of growth rates. We use “acceleration” to refer to an increase in the rate of growth, such that a 2x acceleration means that 2 years of historical progress is made in 1 year. If AECI’s historical trend was 15 points/year, then increasing to 30 points/year implies an acceleration rate of 2 (it takes 1 year to achieve 2 years’ progress at the old rate). For an exponentially growing variable, the acceleration rate is the ratio of growth rates. If a variable is growing 3x/year, then to make 2 years of progress in 1 year the growth rate must be (32)x/yr = 9x/yr (and acceleration can be written as ln(9)/ln(3) = 2). Since October 2025, benchmark scores for internal models have been growing at around twice their historical rate. Benchmark scores of Anthropic’s models, as measured by AECI (Anthropic’s version of the Epoch Capabilities Index), have accelerated 1.9x [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x] since October 2025. Put another way, Anthropic appears to have made as much progress on benchmarks in the past year as they did between October 2023 and October 2025 (roughly, Claude 2.1 to Sonnet 4.5): Our estimated acceleration is greater than that reported in the Haiku 5.5 system card (1.7x) primarily because of the inclusion of data on newer unreleased models, explained further below. We investigated the robustness of these results to different choices of benchmark inclusion, model dating, model inclusion, and benchmark saturation. Robustness analyses find acceleration rates between 1.1x and 2.9x. We would be surprised if the true evolution of benchmark scores (e.g. as measured by an improved version of AECI) showed no acceleration or acceleration above 3x. See our appendix section for details. The acceleration is not driven by an acceleration in the scale of training compute. We received convincing evidence that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scale of training compute. Further details on this evidence were redacted. Interviews and surveys are consistent with AI usage driving this doubling in the pace of capabilities progress. We have many lines of evidence relevant to AI’s contribution to progress in different parts of the model training pipeline, including interviews, self-reported uplift, headcount, lines of code, experiment usage, and qualitative reflections from leadership. We highlight three important unredacted sources. First, both METR and Anthropic interviewed many researchers in detail about the degree of overall acceleration in their area of work attributable to AI use (see details in the appendix below). Our overall impression was a quite wide range of estimates, but centered around a 2x acceleration. Some quotes, with sensitive details redacted, are in the appendix. Second, Anthropic also shared data on self-reported uplift due to AI from a variety of sources. The most recent data is from a series of Slack polls, where staff use reactions to vote on their estimated speedup from the most recent model at the time. We consider this to be only very loose evidence, as the responses reflect low-effort consideration. Nevertheless, we observe consistent growth in these self-reports, and very high levels (reaching 12x in October 2026), as shown in the chart below. Note that individual uplift/speedup estimates do not correspond to acceleration rates. Sustaining a particular growth rate in outputs like model capabilities generally requires a similarly sustained growth in inputs like labor and/or labor productivity to overcome diminishing returns. Achieving a significant acceleration in the overall rate of progress generally requires a significant acceleration of these inputs. We thus care most about whether we see a large change in the growth rate of individual uplift, not the absolute level. Our more detailed analysis of what rate of growth in individual uplift might be needed to explain our estimated acceleration rates in key areas was redacted. Third, we understand that AI is not yet able to make highly significant and fully autonomous contributions to the most important parts of the model training process. However, researchers described significant “signs of life” implying such contributions could occur soon, although with substantial variation in maturity depending on the area. We did not identify any convincing bottlenecks to continued rapid progress. We did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks in algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data that will take effect in the next 12 months. However, our understanding of the status of different bottlenecks changed several times as we got more detailed information, so we are not confident in our current assessment. Anthropic redacted our analysis of a number of specific bottlenecks. Additional redacted evidence was sometimes hard to interpret, but supports sustained and potentially increasing acceleration. We investigated a number of internal metrics and methodologies for measuring acceleration in key areas of the model training pipeline. This included evidence of progress on benchmarks and metrics of algorithmic efficiency and overall model strength in pretraining and RL, as well as improvements to compute utilization, inference efficiency and data efficiency. These investigations included attempts to understand: Different methodological variants of internal metrics. We spent multiple weeks on these investigations, and this is our greatest source of uncertainty. The beliefs of staff on the relevant teams about key internal evidence and estimates of acceleration. Whether other parts of the model training pipeline could be biasing our estimates of acceleration, and where adjustments could be applied. Whether Anthropic could be overfitting to internal metrics. This internal evidence provided support for there being significant acceleration in Anthropic’s model training pipeline. Some of this evidence indicated that acceleration could be above 2x and increasing over time, but there are significant uncertainties about how to interpret it. Process details METR staff assessed how much AI is speeding up AI R&D at Anthropic. METR staff4 (2.5 full-time equivalents) piloted a high-access evaluation at Anthropic to assess the degree to which AI is accelerating AI R&D, and how quickly extreme and risky capabilities may emerge in the near future. Anthropic lists AI R&D acceleration as a key risk indicator in its Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP). In this assessment, we do not pay special attention to the thresholds set in the RSP. Instead, we try to develop a holistic picture of AI-driven acceleration of AI R&D. This engagement started in mid-August, and is distinct from the assessment announced on October 15 by Anthropic. Details of the engagement. The METR staff worked over eleven weeks to independently assess how much AI is accelerating AI R&D at Anthropic. Our assessment focused on three broad questions: Has the growth rate of Anthropic’s internal capabilities accelerated? What share of any acceleration is attributable to AI? Are there important bottlenecks that could slow growth or limit acceleration in the near term? We were additionally scoped to review the AI R&D section of Anthropic’s August 2026 Risk Report, which we are publishing separately. As we describe below, the initial contracted assessment was scoped to include a verification of what percent of compute was allocated to capabilities vs. safety. METR had the ability to request access to any information we believed relevant to understanding AI R&D acceleration, and Anthropic could unilaterally approve or reject our requests. In practice, we often negotiated with Anthropic staff and compromised towards data that was informative, not extremely sensitive, and easy to share. We give more details on what Anthropic shared as well as what it declined to share below, noting that broadly the access provided surpassed our expectations. For this engagement, we did not request or receive access to sample from non-public models. Note that neither METR nor Anthropic intended for this project to involve full “employee-like” access, meaning unmediated access to data, documents, or models. In particular, this project is not the one described in Anthropic’s October 15 update on independent evaluators. Anthropic had unilateral redaction rights over all non-public information in this report. We had a unilateral right to disclose: the existence and general terms of the review and redaction process, whether Anthropic exercised redaction rights, whether or not any findings depended significantly on redacted information, the level of access provided. For security reasons, we worked on Anthropic devices for the duration of this assessment. Anthropic provided free tokens for this assessment, which we primarily used for AI-assisted data analysis and visualization. Per our standard approach, we did not take payment from Anthropic. This exercise followed METR’s policies for engaging with AI companies. We provide a conflict of interest (COI) disclosure and excerpted contract language in the process transparency disclosures appendix plus the AEF-1 checklist. Details of Anthropic’s redactions. Our ~100-page Full Report attempts to answer the key questions we recently described as crucial to answer in future AI R&D assessments in detail. We summarize the evidence sources we were given, and which we were able to include in this public report, in the table below. Our more detailed breakdown of progress attributable to compute, data and algorithmic progress, other than the key takeaway that “We are confident that the acceleration was not due to acceleration in training compute.” More detailed answers to the limitations questions in our proposal, which would require more discussion of methodological details. Forecasts of metrics for future models. They also made some other more minor redactions throughout, which we attempt to describe in each section of this report. Anthropic described the redactions as “aimed at removing confidential information that could accelerate other AI developers.” Key dates. September 22–October 22: METR iterates on the Risk Report Review and the Full Report with further information. October 22: METR delivers its ~100-page Full Report to Anthropic. METR received a significant amount of private data from Anthropic. METR made extensive requests for information on every part of the AI R&D pipeline, and Anthropic shared more information than was initially scoped for this project, surpassing our expectations. Information was typically shared within a few days of requesting it. A detailed description of the data we had access to was redacted. A summarized version is as follows: Internal benchmark scores and AECI for internal models, plus sample tasks, rubric answers and agent expenditure on those tasks. Historical data on algorithmic efficiency and overall model strength in pretraining and RL, as well as improvements to compute utilization, inference efficiency and data efficiency. Headcount and attribution of progress to specific staff. Training compute metrics in many relevant domains. Internal analysis on relevant open questions. Internal surveys of self-reported AI uplift by team. Lines of code and pull requests across the company and some research teams. AI agent inference spend over time. Internal documents on autonomous research contributions. ~15 interviews with key staff, covering a predefined but wide scope that excluded particularly sensitive topics. In a small number of cases, Anthropic did not provide relevant information when they deemed it too sensitive. Anthropic also offered extensive staff time and expertise to this project. We believe the two staff we worked most closely with are the two highest-context researchers on AI R&D acceleration measurement at Anthropic. Both of these staff met with us frequently for live discussion, and spent substantial time collecting data, doing analysis, and providing feedback. Anthropic canceled a compute allocation component of this assessment. The contracted scope of this project originally included a verification of Anthropic’s compute allocation, especially the allocation between capabilities and safety. However, Anthropic changed the scope of this project midway to exclude compute verification and instead just focus on AI R&D acceleration. This component was canceled before METR came to any substantive conclusions on compute usage at Anthropic. Anthropic stated this was due to wanting to keep the engagement focused on risk assessment for the time being, and that it would revisit compute allocation verification later on. Limitations We report our best guesses at ways in which we could be misinterpreting the evidence. We discuss the main ways we could be making mistakes in our interpretation of the evidence. We highlight: Limitations that result from the structure of this assessment. Limitations that result from incorrect analysis. Limited access may have led us to miss important context or data. Despite the access provided to METR, it is clear that staff-level access would enable a significantly deeper assessment. Our pipeline of information was relatively narrow, and a small number of our requests for data were denied. Being able to read documents on demand, observe internal discussion and debate, and have frequent and diverse conversations would have allowed for a richer view. While we believe we had access to the bulk of relevant information, it is possible we missed important information because we did not know it existed or could not look for it ourselves. Over the course of our exercise, we substantially changed our interpretation of key data as more context was shared with us, in some cases leading to multiple reversals on critical questions. We believe fuller access would have dramatically sped up that process of proper interpretation, and we think there likely remain points which we may have misinterpreted due to insufficient context. Acceleration could be higher than this report estimates. Our best guesses as to how we might be underestimating acceleration: We may have missed recent further acceleration. The rate of growth could be undergoing continuous acceleration, e.g. hyperbolic growth. While we do not see clear evidence of this in the AECI trends, there is other evidence that makes this seem more plausible which Anthropic redacted. If growth is hyperbolic, we are likely underestimating instantaneous acceleration and substantially understating acceleration in the near future. In addition, we observe model-level outcomes only after a model is trained, meaning we observe acceleration in effective R&D with a lag roughly equal to the model’s training time. Automation could be closer than we estimated. We understand that AI cannot yet fully automate substantial parts of Anthropic’s model training pipeline; however, there are “signs of life,” discussed below. It is possible that automation is close, and leads to very rapid acceleration once human bottlenecks are removed. AECI could understate real-world capability impact. We have sparse data on the relationship between benchmark scores and real-world impact. As one example, ECI scores on math have not accelerated substantially, but we are now seeing the resolution of Millennium Prize Problems that have evaded decades of human effort. Real-world impacts may be downstream of capability thresholds that models suddenly pass, leading to sudden impacts that are hard to predict. Acceleration could be lower than this report estimates. Our best guesses as to how we might be overestimating acceleration: Non-AI factors could explain most of the acceleration. It’s possible that the non-AI factors explain all or most of the recent acceleration. This implies we have less reason to expect high future growth or future accelerations. Acceleration might be limited to well-specified tasks. Much of the evidence we looked at measures performance on well-specified tasks that are easy to grade automatically or with a language model. If recent models have been growing more quickly on “clean” tasks than on “messy” tasks (relative to historical relative growth rates), then we may be overstating the acceleration in real-world impact. For instance, recent progress may be overfitting to the types of tasks which are included in AECI. Our acceleration numbers could be overstated if the historical rate of growth was unusually low. If progress historically was below its normal or natural rate due to temporary factors, this could lead us to overestimate the amount of acceleration. As we describe in an appendix, Anthropic models had a lower historical growth rate on AECI than the broader industry frontier before late 2025, which could explain some of the acceleration. Appendices Methodology Redactions in this section. None of this section was redacted, but note that some of the methodological discussion may only apply to the Full Report. We include data from Anthropic internal-only models. This includes the following models (these are the codenames shared with us; we understand they have different internal codenames): Unreleased 2022, which finished training in 2022 Model 2, which finished training in July 2026 Model 3, which finished training in August–September 2026 Model 4, which finished training in September–October 2026 METR’s Full Report includes a forecast for a future model, but this was redacted. We use piecewise linear fits to detect acceleration. We typically estimate time trends by an ordinary least squares fit with a single estimated breakpoint; we then report acceleration as the ratio of the two estimated linear trends. We adopt the best-fitting breakpoint on standard AECI data as our default breakpoint on other graphs, to create a consistent breakpoint throughout this report. However, in some places we consider deviations from this, and test estimated acceleration as per the best fit on each graph. We organize our analysis around 3 growth rates: the historical growth rate, the current growth rate and the counterfactual growth rate. We want to assess the degree to which AI automation is speeding up AI progress. For any measure of progress (e.g. model capabilities as measured by AECI), we can estimate three numbers: Historical growth rate: the growth rate prior to a detected trend change. Current growth rate: the growth rate as of October 2026. Counterfactual growth rate: the growth rate as of October 2026, if Anthropic could not use AI. The first two are observable quantities. The counterfactual growth rate we can only guess at. The following plot illustrates these measures on illustrative data: It is important to distinguish between instantaneous acceleration due to AI, as we have defined it, and cumulative acceleration due to AI, i.e. what fraction of overall progress since some point in time (e.g. October 2025) can be attributed to AI. Some interviews and documents are implicitly or explicitly discussing cumulative acceleration, though we generally expect cumulative acceleration to be lower than instantaneous acceleration, due to non-AI acceleratory factors in 2025, and due to the growing influence of AI over time. In the Full Report, we organize indirect evidence with a simple accounting framework. We want to understand if there has been an acceleration in overall capabilities due to AI R&D. To reach our subjective conclusions, we organized our evidence using the following accounting framework, but all relevant usage of it was redacted. Arrows into a box indicate that box is a function of the preceding boxes, so for example, pretraining strength is a function of algorithms, data quality, and training compute. We use the term RL to include all contributions not included in pretraining. This framework lets us start at the right (capabilities) and determine whether there has been an acceleration. Then we can go back one level to see if there has been an acceleration in pretraining or RL, and then go back one further level to see what inputs are causing that acceleration. This allows us to get a deeper understanding of what is happening to the inputs. In the Full Report, analyses were all documented in an accompanying notebook and dashboard. For reproducibility we maintained a notebook and dashboard with all results in the Full Report. Where feasible we included references to the notebook or dashboard, and most charts had a “stamp” which identified their provenance. Benchmark scores (AECI) AECI appendix overview. We expand on the main AECI analysis in a few ways. We explain the methodology behind our main estimation of a 1.9x acceleration in AECI. We show the degree of estimated acceleration varies based on reasonable alternative analysis choices: Varying the link function: 1.1x–2.9x. Varying the snapshots used: 1.9x–2.2x. Varying the benchmarks used: 1.9x–2.2x. Varying the regularizer used: 1.9x–2.1x. We explain why these results differ from AECI estimates in previous Anthropic system cards. We go into detail on potential problems with AECI such as: Anthropic’s internal benchmarks are increasingly saturated: Model 4 achieves greater than 50% on all the AECI benchmarks on which it was tested. However, measured acceleration appears reasonably robust to saturation concerns. Token spend may be too low to maximally elicit models. The logistic link function could be misspecified on a few benchmarks. However, on the whole we think it is a reasonable approximation. There are various reasons why an acceleration in benchmark scores could overstate or understate an acceleration in real-world impacts. Redactions in this section. This section was very minimally redacted by Anthropic. The only information redacted was: The names of specific benchmarks. One graph that shows AECI results for a subset of models chosen on the basis of information that is redacted. Methodological details on AECI estimation. We use Epoch’s public code to estimate AECI values for each model. We generate 95% confidence intervals via bootstrap by drawing benchmark scores with replacement, stratified by model. Our underlying data includes the AECI scores of many snapshots per model. These snapshots differ in both dates and AECI scores. For publicly released models, we include the snapshot that was publicly released and the date that snapshot was available for use by most Anthropic employees. For example, if a model has two snapshots: one available to Anthropic employees on November 10 and one available to Anthropic employees on November 20, and the second snapshot was released publicly on December 1, then our procedure would assign November 20 as the release date. We think there are many reasonable alternative dating procedures (e.g. at first snapshot release instead of last snapshot), which are shown below in one of the robustness exercises. For models that are never released, we include snapshots that received substantial internal usage and the date most Anthropic employees could use them. A specific concern in measuring acceleration with AECI is benchmarks with many broken tasks, or benchmarks with a fat-tailed distribution of task difficulty. The logistic link function assumes exponential tails of task difficulty; if we instead had a fat-tailed distribution of task difficulty, this would mean that going from 98% to 99% requires more AECI points than going from 80% to 90% (the logistic assumes they are approximately equally difficult). A fat-tailed distribution of task difficulty could cause us to underestimate acceleration; as described above, using cauchit or log-log link functions (which model the last few tasks in a benchmark as particularly difficult) results in acceleration estimates of 2.8x and 2.9x, respectively. We perform a simple diagnostic test for task difficulty. For each of the 15 benchmarks used for Model 4 in AECI, we compared a model’s estimated AECI against the model’s log-odds score on that benchmark. If the AECI assumptions are satisfied, meaning task difficulty is logistic in a model’s latent ability, then we would expect each plot to be linear. If there are many broken tasks or a fat-tailed distribution of difficulty, then we would expect these fits to be concave (we would expect a convex fit if there are disproportionately many easy tasks). We noticed there are 3 of 15 benchmarks with notably flat or concave fits. When we re-estimate AECI for all models without those 3 suspicious benchmarks, Model 4’s score increases by 1 point, from 178.6 to 179.7. An acceleration in benchmark scores may fail to track acceleration in real-world impact. Ideally we want to know the real-world value, or potential impact, of each model, not its benchmark scores. If real-world impact is smoothly related to benchmark scores, then we should expect an acceleration in AECI to be associated with an equivalent acceleration in real-world effects.5 There are a number of reasons why acceleration in AECI may fail to track acceleration in the real-world impact of model capabilities: If real-world impact is a convex function of benchmark scores, e.g. if impact depends on crossing a capability threshold, then AECI would understate real-world acceleration. In some domains we have seen a steady increase in benchmark scores accompanied by sudden accelerations in real-world impacts, e.g. impacts on the rate of discoveries in cybersecurity or math (ref). If the benchmarks in AECI cover only a subset of capabilities, and the real-world impact has diminishing returns in those capabilities, then AECI could overstate real-world acceleration. For example, suppose AECI primarily measures a model’s ability to solve formal problems, but there are diminishing real-world returns in that ability; then we might observe an acceleration in AECI without an acceleration in real-world impact. Overall, we are confident there has been at least a modest acceleration in the growth of benchmark scores.
